title: Control Plane Handoff and Fallback Modes: Hosted / Dedicated / Private
content:
Purpose and intent:
This note explores an alternative framing for control-plane handoff and request-level fallback for the three deployment modes (hosted, dedicated, private). Goal: produce small, testable routing patterns that preserve tenant isolation guarantees while enabling predictable graceful degradation across regions and capacity tiers.

Context and motivation:
- We frequently hit two sets of operational surprises: (1) silent capacity saturation that produces tail latency spikes, and (2) control-plane divergence when private deployments apply custom firewall/NAT rules.
- Existing docs cover tenancy boundaries and routing surfaces at a high level; this draft focuses on the handoff semantics (who owns routing decisions at each hop) and explicit fallback transitions for requests.

Glossary (how I use terms here):
- Edge Router (ER): global ingress (hosted) or customer's LB (private/dedicated).
- Local Control Plane (LCP): per-region control plane that can make routing choices (scale, model variant).
- Global Control Plane (GCP): centralized routing policy store (hosted control plane).
- Handoff: transfer of routing decision authority from ER to LCP/GCP.
- Fallback: deterministic alternative path when the primary target is unavailable or violating SLOs.

Handshake and Handoff Modes (new framing)
Mode A - GCP-first (default for hosted):
- ER performs a minimal health check then queries GCP policy service for routing target (model endpoint id + region preference).
- GCP returns a primary endpoint + explicit fallback list (by priority) + TTL for policy cache.
- ER routes to primary; on connection failure or 5xx, ER attempts next fallback in list.
- Advantage: unified policy, fast global policy updates.
- Risk: ER → GCP chattiness during outages; mitigations: local policy cache, exponential backoff.

Mode B - LCP-first (default for dedicated):
- ER uses LCP discovery (SRV/DNS or Consul) and routes locally; LCP owns model variant selection and can spill to other regions per configured affinity rules.
- GCP is eventually consistent and used for non-urgent policy updates.
- Fallback: LCP can instruct ER to reroute to a sibling region via a signed handoff token.
- Advantage: low-latency local decisions, better for committed capacity.
- Risk: policy drift; mitigation: heartbeat reconciliation and mismatch alerting.

Mode C - Customer-Controlled (private):
- ER typically is customer's LB; minimal outbound connections allowed. Handoff occurs via a signed webhook or signed JWT-based policy blob retrieved by ER from customer's internal control plane.
- Fallback behavior must respect customer egress policies (no automatic cross-region unless allowed).
- Provide an explicit "degraded proxy" option: forward to a lightweight private inference proxy (on-prem) that responds with limited functionality rather than failing hard.

New pattern: Progressive Handoff + Fallback Graph
- Each routing decision returns a small directed fallback graph instead of a flat list. Graph nodes are labeled with: endpoint-id, isolation domain (tenant-pool / single-tenant), max-routes (how many hops allowed), and cost-score.
- ER/LCP can walk the graph with domain checks; graph edges include a "policy-eval" predicate (e.g., "latency<150ms && tokens_left>64").
- Benefit: richer guidance for graceful degradation (example: shift from multi-tenant, high-throughput pool → single-tenant warm container → cached-prefix-only responder).

ASCII sequence example (GCP-first, fallback to queued-proxy):
ER -> GCP: GetRoute(tenant=acme, model=v2)
GCP -> ER: RouteGraph(primary=A, fallback=B->C)
ER -> A: POST /invoke (conn timeout) -> ECONNRESET
ER -> B: POST /invoke (returns 503 overloaded)
ER -> C: POST /queued-proxy (accepts request, returns queue-id 3)
ER -> GCP: EmitTelemetry(route=A failed, route=B overloaded, used=C)

Isolation boundaries and guarantees
- Hard guarantees (must enforce): tenant-data egress, tenant compute isolation for single-tenant contracts, and audit trail (signed routing decisions).
- Soft guarantees (operational): prefer single-tenant endpoints for paid tier, fallback into MT pools only when explicitly allowed.
- Implementation knobs:
  - Signed routing tokens: include tenant-id, allowed-mode (mt|st), expiry, and request nonce. ER and endpoint validate token before accepting run.
  - Route tagging: GCP issues tags used by infra to attach networking policy (egress labels, netpol).

Failure modes and mitigations (practical):
1) GCP unreachable from ER (partial network outage):
  - ER uses locally cached RouteGraph plus stale-while-revalidate TTL; if cache expired, ER applies "safe-fail" policy: route to local queued-proxy or return 503 with helpful retry headers.
2) Endpoint silently degrades (e.g., high tail latency):
  - ER monitors tail-latency per-endpoint using a sliding window; upon breach, mark endpoint as soft-failed and walk fallback graph. Send golden metrics to GCP for policy decision.
3) Private deployment forbids cross-region calls:
  - Fallback graph must be annotated with "egress_allowed" boolean. ER respects it; if false, move to next allowed node or use degraded proxy.

Operational telemetry and audit
- Emit three event types for each handoff: RouteDecision, FallbackTrigger, FinalOutcome.
- Each event contains: timestamp, tenant-id (hashed in hosted mode), route-graph-v, chosen-node-id, latency, error-code, token-id.
- Retain detailed telemetry for 30 days (hosted) and 90 days for enterprise customers per SLAs.

Rollout plan for introducing signed RouteGraphs (experiment plan):
- Phase 0 (lab): implement RouteGraph proto and local evaluation lib; unit tests, chaos injection tests in staging.
- Phase 1 (canary): GCP-first mode only. Enable signed graphs for 5% of hosted traffic; validate cache behavior and ER token validation.
- Phase 2 (dedicated): enable LCP-first mode with optional signed handoff tokens between LCPs across regions; pick 2 dedicated customers for pilot where we can coordinate egress rules.
- Phase 3 (private): provide a "policy blob" export that customers can import into their LBs; test fallback proxy with one air-gapped pilot.

Open questions / tradeoffs (items for architecture review meeting):
- Should RouteGraph evaluation be deterministic (same result everywhere) or allow ER to re-weight edges based on local telemetry? (tradeoff: consistency vs. responsiveness)
- How large can the graph be before ER memory/cpu become a concern? (we should cap edges to N=6)
- Token format: JWT vs. mac-signed binary blob? (JWT simpler for customers, binary smaller over wire)
- Billing implications: when fallback moves to cheaper MT pool, how to attribute cost accurately?

Action items and TODOs:
- [ ] Draft RouteGraph proto and push to gh: routing-proto (owner: Raj)
- [ ] Prototype queued-proxy binary with token validation (owner: Sofia)
- [ ] Run a chaos test where GCP is rate-limited and observe ER behavior (owner: Ava)
- [ ] Write SLOs for fallback transitions (keep error amplification < 3x) (owner: Liam)

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally lean and operationally-focused. I'm pushing a new abstraction (RouteGraph) to reduce brittle ad-hoc fallback lists. The idea is to make the routing decision richer but still cheap to evaluate at the edge.
- Please comment on whether the signed token requirement is feasible for private customers with strict egress rules; specifically, is the webhook model acceptable?

References and supporting links:
- Confluence: CONFLUENCE-PLAT-4567 (control plane design doc)
- Jira: JIRA-PLAT-1829 (route token workstream)
- Prototype PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/routing-prototypes/pull/42

Appendix: quick decision table (one-liner guidance)
- Hosted: use GCP-first, enable cache + queued-proxy; default: allow mt fallbacks for free-tier only.
- Dedicated: use LCP-first, signed handoff tokens for cross-region spill; prefer local single-tenant when available.
- Private: customer-controlled; expose policy blobs and a degraded-proxy binary; do not auto-spill across customer egress boundaries.

End of doc.
